A 35-year-old woman comes to the office due to frequent urination.  She describes drinking excessive amounts of water due to unquenchable thirst.  She does not take any medications.  Her blood glucose level is 86 mg/dL.  A standard water deprivation test is performed, and urine osmolality is measured hourly.  After 3 hours of water deprivation, the patient's plasma osmolality is 298 mOsm/kg, and desmopressin is administered subcutaneously.  The results of the test are presented in the table below.

Time (hours)1234
(1 hour after desmopressin)
Urine osmolality (mOsm/kg)90100100790

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌
explanation:
Vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone [ADH]) is released from the posterior pituitary in response to increased plasma osmolality.  ADH activates Gs protein-coupled V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting duct principal cells, increasing the number of aquaporin 2 channels on the luminal membrane, which allows water reabsorption into the hypertonic medullary interstitium.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) results from either deficient ADH secretion (central DI) or renal resistance to ADH (nephrogenic DI).  In both, impaired free water reabsorption causes polyuria with dilute urine, and the resulting rise in plasma osmolality stimulates thirst and compensatory polydipsia.

Because primary polydipsia also causes polyuria with dilute urine, a water deprivation test followed by desmopressin (DDAVP, a V2 receptor agonist) is used to distinguish these conditions.  Water deprivation raises plasma osmolality, which normally triggers ADH release and urine concentration; once plasma osmolality is elevated (eg, >295 mOsm/kg), desmopressin is given to assess the renal response to ADH.

This patient's urine osmolality remained low despite an elevated plasma osmolality, indicating an inability to concentrate urine (ie, DI).  When desmopressin was administered, urine osmolality increased markedly (although submaximally due to medullary washout from chronic polyuria), demonstrating an intact renal response to ADH; therefore, the defect is deficient ADH secretion (central DI).

(Choices B and C)  In nephrogenic DI, the kidneys respond poorly to ADH, so urine osmolality changes little after desmopressin.  In complete nephrogenic DI, urine remains inappropriately dilute throughout the test.  In partial nephrogenic DI, urine osmolality rises slowly as plasma osmolality increases during water deprivation but typically remains <500 mOsm/kg.  In contrast, this patient's urine did not concentrate during water deprivation but concentrated markedly after desmopressin.

(Choice D)  Relief of bilateral urinary obstruction (eg, Foley catheterization in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia) may result in post-obstructive diuresis as the kidneys excrete retained urea, sodium, and water; obstruction-induced tubular injury can also impair urine concentration.  This patient has no history suggesting urinary obstruction.

(Choice E)  In primary polydipsia, excessive water intake suppresses ADH secretion, causing polyuria with dilute urine and low-normal plasma osmolality.  Because ADH secretion and the renal response to ADH are intact, urine osmolality increases during water deprivation (but remains submaximal due to washout of the medullary osmotic gradient), with little further increase after desmopressin.  Primary polydipsia is often associated with psychiatric disorders or medication-induced xerostomia.

Educational objective:Patients with diabetes insipidus (DI) are unable to concentrate their urine in response to dehydration.  Following desmopressin administration during the water deprivation test, urine osmolality increases markedly in central DI (intact renal response to ADH) but changes little in nephrogenic DI.  In primary polydipsia, urine concentrates during water deprivation alone.​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌
